name: Arughat
blurb: A busy bazaar town on both banks of the Budhi Gandaki and the old starting point of the Manaslu trek. Buses and jeeps now pass through on the way to Soti Khola and Machha Khola.
tip: Bring the cash for the whole trek from Kathmandu; do not count on a cash machine here or anywhere beyond.

name: Soti Khola
blurb: A roadside village at a side stream of the Budhi Gandaki, and the trailhead until the road was pushed on to Machha Khola. Starting here adds a day of walking, much of it on or beside the jeep track.

name: Machha Khola
blurb: The usual start of the Manaslu and Tsum treks: a line of lodges above the Budhi Gandaki where the bus and jeep road from Kathmandu ends for most travellers. The name means fish stream.
tip: Keep your permits and a few photocopies at the top of your pack; the first checkpoint is a day ahead at Jagat.

name: Khorlabesi
blurb: A small farming village on a river terrace about an hour and a half above Machha Khola. Its few lodges make a quieter first stop, and the landslide scars around it show how unstable this stretch of the gorge is.

name: Tatopani
blurb: A hot spring piped into stone spouts beside the trail between Khorlabesi and Dobhan, with a couple of simple lodges. Not the larger Tatopani on the Kali Gandaki.

name: Dobhan
blurb: A cluster of lodges where a side river joins the Budhi Gandaki, a little under halfway from Machha Khola to Jagat. A sensible place to stop if the long second day proves too much.

name: Jagat
blurb: A stone-paved village where the Manaslu Conservation Area office checks permits and the restricted area begins. Most trekkers spend their second night here. Not the Jagat on the Annapurna Circuit.
tip: Hand over the restricted-area permit and the conservation-area permit together; the office logs every group.

name: Philim
blurb: A large Gurung village on a sunny shelf above the river, with a school, a police checkpost and fields of maize and millet. The trail to Tsum leaves the main valley about an hour and a half further north.

name: Deng
blurb: A few lodges and houses at the upper end of the bamboo gorge, where Kutang, the lower part of Nubri, begins. From here on, mani walls and chortens line the trail.

name: Ghap
blurb: A hamlet with finely carved mani walls beside the river, roughly halfway between Deng and Namrung. Above it the trail enters tall fir and rhododendron forest for the long climb to Namrung.

name: Namrung
blurb: The entrance to upper Nubri, on a shelf above the gorge, with a checkpost and some of the better lodges on the circuit. Siringi Himal and Ganesh Himal come into view here for the first time.
tip: A flash flood in September 2026 destroyed a bridge near the village and a temporary crossing was put in; ask ahead about its condition after rain.

name: Lho
blurb: A large Nubri village below Ribung Gompa, with a full view of Manaslu's twin summits up the valley. Sunrise on the mountain from the monastery hill is the reason many groups spend a night here.

name: Shyala
blurb: A cluster of newer lodges on an open terrace ringed by peaks: Himalchuli and Ngadi Chuli to the south, Manaslu ahead and the Ganesh range behind. An alternative overnight stop to Lho.

name: Sama Gaun
blurb: The main village of Nubri, a long street of stone houses below the Manaslu glacier and the standard place for a rest day. Side trips lead to Birendra Tal, Pungyen Gompa and Manaslu Base Camp.
tip: Spend two nights here. Walk high during the day and come back down to sleep; the next three nights are all higher.

name: Pungyen Gompa
blurb: A small monastery on a yak pasture beneath the east face of Manaslu, up a side valley between Shyala and Sama Gaun. Published heights run from 3,870 m to a little over 4,000 m; the climb from the main trail is roughly 500 m.

name: Birendra Tal
blurb: A milky-blue lake at the foot of the Manaslu glacier, under an hour's walk from Sama Gaun. Blocks of ice fall into the water in the warmer months. Usually given as 3,691 m, though some maps show it lower.

name: Manaslu Base Camp
blurb: The expedition base on a moraine shelf beside the Manaslu glacier, a steep climb of about 1,270 m from Sama Gaun. Tents fill it in September and October. There and back is a full, hard day.
tip: Treat it as an optional extra, not the default rest-day walk, and turn back if you are slow or cloud comes in.

name: Samdo
blurb: The last permanent village before the Larkya La, settled by families who crossed from Tibet after 1959. Trails north from here lead to the old trade passes on the border.

name: Dharamsala
blurb: The last shelter before the Larkya La: a few stone huts and rows of tents with shared rooms, open only in the trekking seasons. It is cold, basic and often full in October.
tip: Arrive by midday to be sure of a bed, eat early and pack for a 3 to 4 am start.

name: Larkya La
blurb: The high point of the Manaslu Circuit, a long, gradual crossing over moraine and not a sharp notch. The sign at the top reads 5,106 m; some maps give 5,160 m. The west side drops steeply towards Bhimtang.
tip: Be over the top by late morning. Wind and cloud build after midday and there is almost no shelter on either side.

name: Bhimtang
blurb: A broad meadow of lodges beside a glacier moraine, with the first beds after the pass. Manaslu, Himlung and Cheo Himal ring the skyline. Older sources list it at 3,590 m.

name: Gho
blurb: A cluster of lodges where the forest of the Dudh Khola valley gives way to farmland, about four hours below Bhimtang. It lies in Manang district, inside the Annapurna Conservation Area.

name: Tilije
blurb: A large village of stone houses and apple orchards on the Dudh Khola, and a common last night on the Manaslu Circuit. A rough jeep track now links it to the Annapurna Circuit road at Dharapani, an hour and a half below.

name: Lokpa
blurb: The first stop on the Tsum trail, a couple of lodges in pine forest high above the meeting of the Siyar Khola and the Budhi Gandaki. Ahead lies the roughest stretch of the route, through the gorge to Chumling.

name: Chumling
blurb: The main village of lower Tsum, on a slope above the Siyar Khola, with small monasteries and stone-walled fields of maize and potatoes. On a clear day Shringi Himal stands above the houses.

name: Chhokang Paro
blurb: Twin villages, Chhokang and Paro, on a flat shelf at the entrance to upper Tsum. The valley opens out here after the steep climb from the gorge, with Ganesh Himal to the south and Himalchuli behind you.
tip: The climb from the river brings you above 3,000 m in a morning; walk it slowly and notice how you sleep.

name: Rachen Gompa
blurb: A large walled nunnery on the flat valley floor of upper Tsum, founded in the early 1900s and now the largest nunnery in the valley. Visitors can usually look round the prayer hall, and simple rooms are sometimes available.

name: Nile
blurb: The last village with lodges in upper Tsum, across the Siyar Khola from Chhule. Stone houses keep livestock on the ground floor, and barley and potato fields fill the valley floor around them.

name: Mu Gompa
blurb: The largest monastery in Tsum, on a bare hillside at the head of the valley with a wide view back down it. The monks run very basic guest rooms. Beyond lie only yak pastures and the old trade passes to Tibet.
tip: Bring a warm sleeping bag and expect simple food. For more comfort, sleep in Nile and visit as a day walk.

name: Gumba Lungdang
blurb: A small nunnery on a forested spur above Dumje, off the main Tsum trail, facing the Ganesh Himal range. It is the base for the long day walk to Ganesh Himal Base Camp at about 4,200 m.
